prompt: How many cells does **Highlight Cells Rules › Greater Than** `1000` colour on `Sales[Revenue]`?
hint: `=COUNTIF(Sales[Revenue], ">1000")` counts them.

prompt: **Top 10 Items** on `Sales[Revenue]` colours 11 cells. Why?
hint: Look at the tenth-largest value and how many sales have it.

choices.text: Excel counts the header as one of the ten
choices.why: The rule applies to H2:H109, which has no header in it.

choices.text: A tie: two sales share the tenth value, 1,456
choices.why: Right. The rule colours every value at least as large as the tenth.

choices.text: The rule rounds 10 percent of 108 up to 11
choices.why: That would be Top 10 %; Top 10 Items counts values, not a percentage.

choices.text: One sale is counted twice because it is in two channels
choices.why: Each sale has exactly one channel, and the rule looks only at revenue.

prompt: **Above Average** colours 37 of the 108 sales, not about half. What explains it?
hint: Where do the largest sales sit compared with the rest?

choices.text: A few large wholesale orders pull the average up above most sales
choices.why: Right. The average is R$ 476.80 and most sales are far smaller.

choices.text: The rule uses the median, not the average
choices.why: Above Average uses the average; the median would split the sales near half.

choices.text: Excel leaves out the sales of 2026 from the average
choices.why: The average is of the whole selected range.

choices.text: Sales exactly at the average are left uncoloured, and there are many
choices.why: No sale is exactly R$ 476.80; the cause is the shape of the data.

prompt: **Duplicate Values** on `Sales[Sale]` colours nothing. What does that tell you?
hint: Lesson 1 section 06 named what kind of column `Sale` is.

choices.text: The rule is broken on text values
choices.why: On `Sales[Customer]` the same rule colours almost every cell.

choices.text: Each code appears once, as a key's values do
choices.why: Right. A key identifies one row each, so no value repeats.

choices.text: All the sales were made on different days of the year
choices.why: The rule looks at the codes in the column, not at dates.

choices.text: Nothing; the rule only works on columns of numbers
choices.why: It works on text, which is why it is a quick check on a key.

prompt: What does a conditional format do that a fill painted by hand does not?
hint: Change the number in the cell and watch both.

choices.text: It colours every cell of the sheet
choices.why: It colours only the cells the rule is true for.

choices.text: It makes the value easier to sort
choices.why: Sorting depends on the value, which neither changes.

choices.text: It changes the value stored in the cell
choices.why: A format never changes a value; it only decides how it looks.

choices.text: It follows the value
choices.why: Right. A painted fill stays put when the value changes; a rule follows it.

prompt: The rule `=G2="Wholesale"`, with no dollar sign, is applied to A2:H109. What gets coloured?
hint: Move the formula one column right, as a fill would, and see what it asks.

choices.text: Every wholesale row, from A to H
choices.why: That needs $G2. Without it, column B asks about H, column C about I, and so on.

choices.text: Column A cells of the wholesale rows
choices.why: Right. Column A is the only one whose moved formula still reads Channel.

choices.text: Only the G cells holding Wholesale
choices.why: Cell G2 would ask about M2, which is empty.

choices.text: Nothing, because the rule has an error
choices.why: The formula is valid; it asks the wrong cells, which is why no error warns you.

prompt: The rule `=$G$2="Wholesale"` is applied to A2:H109, and G2 holds `Wholesale`. How many cells are coloured?
hint: Every cell asks the same question about the same cell.

prompt: A rule written for A2 as `=$G2="Wholesale"` covers A2:H109. Which formula does cell D7 effectively ask?
hint: The row moves with the cell; the column after a dollar sign stays.

choices.text: `=$G2="Wholesale"`
choices.why: That is A2's question. The row is relative and moves to 7.

choices.text: `=$J7="Wholesale"`
choices.why: $G is fixed, so the column does not move three places.

choices.text: `=$G7="Wholesale"`
choices.why: Right: the channel of D7's own row.

choices.text: `=D7="Wholesale"`
choices.why: The rule never tests the cell itself unless the formula names it.

prompt: In `=$G2="Wholesale"`, the dollar sign fixes the ___, so every cell of a row tests the same field.
hint: A letter, not a number.

prompt: Why does the lesson put 1500 in a cell named `Threshold` instead of typing it into the rule?
hint: Who has to open the Rules Manager to move the line?

choices.text: Rules refuse numbers larger than 999
choices.why: A rule takes any number; the lesson typed 1000 into one in section 02.

choices.text: A name makes the rule recalculate faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: So the line moves by typing in a cell
choices.why: Right. Anybody reading the sheet can try 1000 or 2000 without knowing where rules live.

choices.text: Because Excel needs every rule to refer to another sheet
choices.why: The Threshold cell sits on the same sheet.

prompt: On the `By month` grid one colour scale over B2:D19 shows `Shop` pale all the way down. How do you see the shop's own strong and weak months?
hint: Decide which values each cell is measured against.

choices.text: Apply a three-colour scale instead of a two-colour one
choices.why: More colours on the same scale still measure the shop against wholesale.

choices.text: Give each column a separate scale, as three rules
choices.why: Right. Each channel is then shaded against its own smallest and largest month.

choices.text: Delete the Wholesale column
choices.why: That loses data to fix a view; separate scales keep both.

choices.text: Sort the grid by Shop
choices.why: Sorting moves rows; the scale still compares every cell with 4,538.

prompt: With the default three coloured arrows on `Sales[Revenue]`, how many sales get the red arrow?
hint: Below 33% of the distance from 34 to 2,120.

prompt: In the default icon set, what does *67 percent* mean for `Sales[Revenue]`?
hint: The line falls at 1,431.62.

choices.text: The 67th percentile: two thirds of the sales lie below it
choices.why: That would be the Percentile type. Here 97 of 108 sales lie below the line.

choices.text: 67% of the largest sale, 2,120
choices.why: That would be 1,420.40, and the minimum would play no part.

choices.text: A share of the distance from smallest to largest
67% of the total revenue, 51,494
choices.why: No single sale comes near that; every sale would get the red arrow.

prompt: Which format suits a column of monthly totals where the question is *which is bigger, and by how much*?
hint: What does the eye compare most easily?

choices.text: Data bars
choices.why: Right. A bar is a length, and lengths are the easiest thing to compare.

choices.text: Three coloured arrows
choices.why: Arrows suggest a direction of change, which a total does not have.

choices.text: Duplicate Values
choices.why: That answers whether a value repeats.

choices.text: Text that Contains
choices.why: That tests text, and these are numbers.

prompt: In the `By month` grid, in which of these months did the shop (`Shop`) sell nothing? Choose all that apply.
hint: A scale per column makes the empty months of each channel stand out.

choices.text: May 2025
choices.why: The Shop cell for May 2025 is 0.

choices.text: June 2025
choices.why: The shop sold 76 that month; it was Online that sold nothing.

choices.text: August 2025
choices.why: 0 in the Shop column.

choices.text: April 2026
choices.why: 0, in the same month wholesale sold nothing either.

choices.text: February 2026
choices.why: The shop's best month: 274.

prompt: Match each question to the format that answers it.
hint: Each kind of format answers one kind of question.

pairs.right: A fill on those cells, and nothing on the rest

pairs.left: How big is each month's total, compared with the others?
Where in a grid are the high and low values?
Did each customer buy more or less than last year?
pairs.right: Arrows on a column holding the change

right_distractors: Arrows on a column of revenue

prompt: A sheet marks good months green and bad months red, with nothing else in the cells. What is wrong with it?
hint: Think about every reader, and about a printer.

choices.text: Green and red are too bright to print on most office printers
choices.why: Brightness is not the issue; telling the two apart is.

choices.text: Only colour carries the meaning
choices.why: Right. Around one man in twelve has trouble telling red from green; a second signal, a shape, a word or a difference in lightness, fixes it.

choices.text: Excel cannot use green in a conditional format
choices.why: Any colour can be used.

choices.text: Months should never be coloured at all
choices.why: Colouring months is fine; colour alone carrying the meaning is the problem.

prompt: What does a flag column such as `=IF([@Revenue]>=Threshold, "Large", "")` give that the colour of the same rule does not?
hint: Lesson 1 said what a formula cannot count.

choices.text: A faster sheet, because colours slow Excel down
choices.why: Speed is not the point; what the flag can be used for is.

choices.text: Nothing; it repeats the colour in words
choices.why: Saying it in words is exactly what makes it usable by formulas, filters and screen readers.

choices.text: A value COUNTIF counts, a filter selects, and a screen reader reads aloud
choices.why: Right, and it survives a paste as values. A colour does none of those.

choices.text: It removes the need for the Threshold cell
choices.why: The flag reads Threshold, just as the rule does.

prompt: The wholesale rows of `Sales` are coloured by `=$G2="Wholesale"`. What does that rule add to the sheet?
hint: Can the reader already read the channel somewhere?

choices.text: Emphasis, not information
choices.why: Right. Column G already says Wholesale on every one of those rows; keep the rule only if wholesale is what this sheet is about.

choices.text: New information that no column holds
choices.why: Column G holds exactly this, in words.

choices.text: A count of wholesale sales, shown in the status bar
choices.why: A format counts nothing; COUNTIF does.

choices.text: A check that every channel is spelt correctly
choices.why: A misspelt channel would simply be left uncoloured, and nothing would say why.

prompt: On `Sales[Revenue]`, a pale fill for `>= 1000` sits above a strong fill for `>= 1500` in the Rules Manager. What does the sheet show?
hint: When two rules set the fill of one cell, which wins?

choices.text: Nine strong cells and nine pale ones
choices.why: That is what the other order shows.

choices.text: All 18 cells pale
choices.why: Right. The 1,000 rule is higher and wins on the fill for all 18; the 1,500 rule loses every time.

choices.text: All 18 cells strong
choices.why: The lower rule never wins a clash on the same property.

choices.text: An error message about overlapping rules
choices.why: Excel says nothing; that is why the order matters.

prompt: Three fill rules on `Sales[Revenue]` should show three grades. Put them in order, top of the Rules Manager first.
hint: The narrower condition goes above the wider one.
trap: With >= 500 on top, every sale of 500 or more is pale and the other two rules never show.

prompt: Where do you see every conditional format rule on a sheet, including ones you did not make?
hint: The list opens on the current selection.

choices.text: Manage Rules, with This Worksheet chosen
choices.why: Right. Only the manager lists them all.

choices.text: Data › Data Validation, on the Settings tab
choices.why: That holds validation rules, which are another thing.

choices.text: Formulas › Name Manager, with every name shown
choices.why: That lists names, such as Threshold, not formats.

choices.text: Right-click a cell › Format Cells › Fill
choices.why: That shows the formats applied by hand.

prompt: You choose **Clear Rules › Clear Rules from Entire Sheet**. What stays?
hint: Clear Rules is about one kind of formatting.

choices.text: Nothing: every format on the sheet is removed
choices.why: Only conditional formats go.

choices.text: The rules, switched off until you turn them on
choices.why: Cleared rules are deleted, not paused.

choices.text: Only the rules inside tables
choices.why: Entire Sheet covers tables too.

choices.text: Fills and fonts applied by hand
choices.why: Right. Clear Rules removes conditional formats only.

prompt: Somebody applies `=$H$2>=1500` to A2:H109 of `Sales`, meaning to colour the large sales. H2 holds 1,456. What is coloured?
hint: Every cell asks about the same cell.

choices.text: The 9 sales of 1,500 or more
choices.why: That needs $H2, so each row asks about its own revenue.

choices.text: Every row, because the rule is about revenue
choices.why: Every cell asks whether H2 is at least 1,500, and it is not.

choices.text: Only cell H2
choices.why: All cells ask the same question; none is singled out.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right. H2, sale S1001, is 1,456, so the one question every cell asks is false.

prompt: A manager wants to see at a glance which customers bought more in 2026 than in the same months of 2025. Which arrangement communicates it?
hint: Arrows mean a direction of change. What has to be in the cells for them to mean that?

choices.text: A colour scale on each customer's 2026 revenue
choices.why: That shows who is big this year, not who grew.

choices.text: A column holding the change per customer, with arrows on it
choices.why: Right. Arrows mean up or down, and here the values are ups and downs.

choices.text: Three coloured arrows on each customer's 2026 revenue
choices.why: The arrows would grade size against the range, which is the lesson's 86 red arrows again.

choices.text: Data bars on the 2025 revenue
choices.why: Bars compare sizes within one year; they say nothing about change.

prompt: With `Threshold` set to 1000, how many cells does the rule `=$H2>=Threshold` colour across A2:H109?
hint: Count the rows first, then remember how many columns each row has.
